growth_story.headline: Estonia raced ahead on a 2000–2007 credit boom, crashed in 2008–09, and after a 2022–24 slump its income per person is back near its 2018 level.
growth_story.arc: After independence, income per person fell hard, by 19.7 percent in 1992 alone, so the 1991–1999 era averaged only 0.2 percent a year despite a quick rebound behind a currency board and fast reforms. From 2000 to 2007 growth averaged 8.5 percent a year, as a credit boom pushed output well above what the IMF judged the economy could sustain. The bust was severe: income per person fell 4.9 percent in 2008 and 14.5 percent in 2009, and wage cuts and budget cuts carried the adjustment while the currency board held. Growth came back in the 2010s, but the 2008–2025 era averages just 0.9 percent, pulled down by that crash and by a second downturn in 2022–2024 that the IMF links to supply shocks, high inflation, rising costs and lost export markets. Income per person peaked in 2021 and, after growth of 1.0 percent in 2025, is still 6.0 percent below that peak and about where it first was in 2018.

threads.title: Currency board and fast reform
threads.text: Income per person fell 7.5 percent in 1991 and 19.7 percent in 1992 after independence, then grew strongly from 1995, including 14.3 percent in 1997. The IMF says the currency board was run skillfully and the budget balanced while growth returned. It also notes a stock market bubble that burst in late 1997 and the Russian financial crisis soon after; income per person dipped 0.7 percent in 1999.

threads.title: Credit boom, then bust
threads.text: Growth of 8.5 percent a year in 2000–2007 rested partly on a credit boom that swelled construction, finance and real estate. Income per person then fell 4.9 percent in 2008 and 14.5 percent in 2009. Fiscal reserves and quick budget measures kept the government funded and supported the currency board.

citations.title: Republic of Estonia: Staff Report for the 2009 Article IV Consultation (IMF Country Report No. 10/4)
citations.quote: Following a credit boom, the Estonian economy is now undergoing a severe recession, although a full-fledged crisis has been avoided.

citations.title: Republic of Estonia: Staff Report for the 2009 Article IV Consultation (IMF Country Report No. 10/4)
citations.quote: Growth in recent years was unsustainably bolstered by a disproportionate rise in nontradable sectors (construction, financial intermediation, real estate), with negative implications for competitiveness.

citations.title: Republic of Estonia: Staff Report for the 2009 Article IV Consultation (IMF Country Report No. 10/4)
citations.quote: Sizable fiscal reserves and swift adjustment measures taken in 2008 and throughout 2009 prevented funding problems of the government and supported the currency board arrangement

threads.title: Weaker exports and productivity
threads.text: Growth averaged 2.1 percent a year in 2006–2015 and 1.4 percent in 2016–2025. The IMF says export performance weakened soon after the 2008–09 crisis, and that declining business dynamism has weighed on productivity.

citations.title: Republic of Estonia: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2024 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: Estonia lost significant export market shares in the last two years and external performance weakened soon after the Global Financial Crisis

citations.title: Republic of Estonia: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2025 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: declining business dynamism has weighed adversely on productivity.

threads.title: The 2022–2024 downturn
threads.text: After a jump of 8.1 percent in 2021, income per person fell three years running: 2.5 percent in 2022, 4.3 percent in 2023 and 0.2 percent in 2024. The IMF ties this to supply shocks and a jump in inflation that left prices and costs above the euro area average. It says higher input costs and trade barriers slowed the rebound.

citations.title: Republic of Estonia: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2024 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: Recent shocks triggered supply side disruptions and a large rise in inflation

citations.title: Republic of Estonia: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2024 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: inflation has now eased but price and cost levels have shifted up compared to the euro area average, hurting competitiveness.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2025 Article IV Consultation with Estonia
citations.quote: higher input costs, a legacy of earlier shocks, global policy uncertainty, and trade barriers are preventing a more vigorous rebound.

threads.title: Defence spending and energy prices
threads.text: In 2025 Estonia raised its defence spending target. The IMF notes that much military equipment is imported, which limits the boost to local output, and that the war in the Middle East is weighing on the outlook through higher energy prices.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 1.0 percent in 2025, the first rise after three years of decline. By mid-2026 the IMF reported faster growth, led by household spending after an income tax change, while exports and investment stayed weak and the war in the Middle East pushed energy prices up.

citations.title: Republic of Estonia: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2026 Article IV Mission

growth_story.tension: The IMF dates a weakening in export performance to soon after the 2008–09 crisis, yet income per person grew every year from 2010 to 2019. Much of the low 0.9 percent average for 2008–2025 comes from two deep falls, in 2008–09 and 2022–24, rather than a decade of weak growth. Also, the IMF history says output per person was far above its pre-independence level by the end of the 1990s, but in these data income per person in 1999 was still a little below 1990 and passed it only in 2000.
